articles.title: India's first imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit lifts off successfully
articles.content: What's New Share DD India September 4, 2026 8:42 AM IST first imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit | satellite in geosynchronous orbit lifts off successfully | India's first imaging satellite India’s first imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit lifts off successfully Author: DD India ISRO’s state-of-the art Earth observation spacecraft, the country’s first ever imaging satellite intended for the Geosynchronous orbit, EOS-05 lifted off from the spaceport here on Friday. Set to provide real-time imagery and help the nation in areas including agriculture, and disaster management, a GSLV-F17 rocket carrying the payload headed into the wide skies carrying the satellite, intended for delivery at the Sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit (Sub-GTO) in the wee hours. After the completion of a smooth 27-hour countdown, which commenced at 23.30 hours on Wednesday, the rocket, with a 2,367 kg payload mass, began its ascent on dot at 2.55 AM from the second launch pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre. The odd hour and rain could not deter the enthusiasm of members of public as many turned up to cheer the launch. While several earth observation satellites operate from low earth orbit (LEO), the EOS-5 satellite is set to hover at an altitude of roughly 36,000 km above earth, which is the geosynchronous orbit and at that level, the satellite will match Earth’s rotational speed. The GSLV-F-17 is the 19th flight of India’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle. The 3-stage, 51.7 meter rocket, with its third stage being cryogenic, has a lift off mass of 420.5 tonne and the over-2,000 kg satellite is ensconced on the rocket nose cone. The GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission is said to be a replacement for the unsuccessful GSLV-F-10/EOS-03 mission of 2021. An onboard computer had aborted that mission at 307 seconds into the flight then. A probe into the post-flight data had indicated that an anomaly in the Cryogenic Upper Stage led to the mission failure, according to ISRO. The pre-dawn launch on Friday follows a gap of nearly 8 months. On January 12 this year, ISRO’s PSLV-C62 rocket carrying 16 satellites failed to place them in the intended orbit after encountering an “anomaly” in the critical third stage of the launch. This was ISRO’s only launch this year and it failed. A similar, previous attempt in May 2025 (PSLV-C61-EOS-09) also did not succeed due to a “motor pressure issue,” and there was a fall in the chamber pressure of the motor case. Days ago, ISRO chairman V Narayanan visited the Tirumala Tirupati Lord Venkateshwara Swamy temple and prayed for the mission’s success. -PTI

articles.title: GSLV-F17 launch a reflection of India's growing space capabilities: PM Modi - ANI News
articles.content: New Delhi [India], September 4 (ANI): Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday hailed the successful launch of ISRO's GSLV-F17 carrying the Advanced Earth Observation Satellite-05 (EOS-05), calling it an "outstanding achievement" and a proud moment for the nation. The GSLV-F17 vehicle successfully and precisely injected EOS-05, also known as the geo-imaging star satellite, into its intended orbit, marking another milestone for India's space programme, ISRO chief V Narayanan announced on Thursday. In a post on X, PM Modi said the mission reflected the "excellence, innovation and growing capabilities" of India's space sector. "Yet another outstanding achievement by ISRO and a proud moment for our nation. The successful launch of GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05, India’s first-ever imaging satellite from Geosynchronous orbit is a reflection of the excellence, innovation and growing capabilities that define India’s space sector," Modi said. The Prime Minister also highlighted the growing collaboration between the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the country's private industry, saying the partnership was strengthening and scaling up India's space programme. "The growing partnership between ISRO and Indian industry is adding new strength and scale to our space programme and expanding India’s capabilities across the entire space ecosystem," he added. Speaking after the successful launch of GSLV-F17, the ISRO chief said the successful mission was a significant achievement for India’s space programme and that the satellite’s health was perfectly alright after its injection into orbit. “I am very happy to announce that the GSLV-F17 vehicle has successfully and precisely injected the Advanced Earth Observation Satellite 05, the geo-imaging satellite, in the intended and required orbit," he said. He added that once EOS-05 is operationalised in orbit, it will become India’s first dedicated imaging satellite from the geo orbit and provide important strategic data for the country. “Today, we have injected the heaviest satellite, 2367 kgs, using this launch vehicle. The health of the satellite is perfectly alright,” the ISRO chief said. ISRO successfully deployed the EOS-05 Earth observation satellite into orbit from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota on Friday, marking another major milestone in India’s space programme. The launch took place from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, SHAR. The launch was carried out on a GSLV-F17 rocket, which is the 19th flight of India’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV), as it carried EOS-05 towards a Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (Sub-GTO). (ANI)

Friday’s launch marked the space agency’s maiden success of 2026. The EOS-05 satellite was successfully placed in the intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit about 18 minutes after it lifted off from the spaceport here, ISRO announced. While several Earth observation satellites operate from low Earth orbit (LEO), the EOS-05 satellite is set to hover at an altitude of roughly 36,000 km above Earth, which is the geosynchronous orbit. At that level, the satellite will match Earth’s rotational speed. At over 2,300 kg, this is the heaviest satellite ever to be carried by a GSLV, and the satellite was successfully placed in its intended trajectory. “The eye in the sky,” as one of the senior scientists involved in the mission described the satellite, is set to provide real-time imagery and help the nation in areas including agriculture and disaster management. articles.title: ISRO Successfully Launches Earth Observation Satellite EOS-05 From Sriharikota
articles.content: National Translate Translate Space Technology / ISRO Successfully Launches Earth Observation Satellite EOS-05 From Sriharikota H Hemanta Pande Browse all articles by Hemanta Pande · 2 hours ago · 2 min read ISRO successfully launched Earth observation satellite EOS-05 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota . Key Points ISRO successfully launched EOS-05, India's first Earth observation satellite in geosynchronous orbit, from Sriharikota. The GSLV-F17 rocket placed the satellite into sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit, enhancing India’s imaging capabilities for disaster management, agriculture, and environmental monitoring. Sriharikota, Sept 4: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched EOS-05, the country’s first imaging satellite designed to operate from a geosynchronous orbit, aboard the GSLV-F17 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre here in the early hours of Friday. ISRO said that the state-of-the-art Earth observation spacecraft EOS-05 was successfully placed into sub-geosynchronous orbit about 18 minutes after it lifted off from the spaceport. The GSLV-F17 mission represents the 19th flight of India’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle series. The vehicle employed a 4-metre diameter composite ogive payload fairing, underscoring ISRO’s growing technological sophistication in launch systems. The launch was conducted from the Second Launch Pad (SLP), reinforcing India’s operational capabilities in handling complex missions. EOS-05 is a state-of-the-art spacecraft designed to provide advanced Earth imaging from geosynchronous orbit, a first for India. Unlike satellites in low Earth orbit, EOS-05’s vantage point allows continuous observation of specific regions, enhancing applications in disaster management, agriculture, urban planning, and environmental monitoring. The mission is expected to significantly strengthen India’s remote sensing programme and expand its role in global Earth observation initiatives. articles.title: ISRO successfully launches Earth observation satellite EOS-05 - The New Indian Express
articles.content: BENGALURU: The GSLV-F17 (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle) carrying EOS-05 executed a textbook launch at 2.55 am on Friday. After setbacks during previous missions, Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) teams worked continuously to ensure the mission's success, with the GSLV-F17 placing the EOS-05 satellite into a Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit at 3.14 am. Friday's launch marked the space agency's maiden success for the year 2026. The EOS-05 is India’s first ever imaging satellite to monitor from Geosynchronous orbit about 36,000 km above the Earth. ISRO teams noted that this is the heaviest satellite ever launched into a geosynchronous orbit, with a lift-off mass of 420.5 tonnes. The 51.7-metre-tall vehicle was launched from the second launch pad of the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota amid light rain. A beaming ISRO chief V Narayanan said, "I am very happy to announce that the GSLV F-17 vehicle has successfully and precisely injected the advanced EOS-05 geo imaging satellite in the intended and required orbit." "This is the 107th launch from Srihariharikota and the 19th mission of GSLV," he said soon after the launch. Narayanan added that this was the second launch of the financial year and the first for ISRO. Six more launches have been targeted for this financial year, including NVS-03. The teams are also working on the Gaganyaan mission, with the first uncrewed mission under the programme scheduled for launch during this financial year, he said. Former ISRO directors Dr K Radhakrishnan, K Kiran Kumar and S Somanath were also present at the launch site, along with teams from the Indian Air Force and the Indian Navy. The GSLV-F17 launch comprised three stages, solid, liquid propulsion and cryogenic. Loud cheers erupted in the launch room when the successful completion of the cryogenic stage was announced by the directors 15 minutes after the launch, overcoming the earlier hiccups faced during the cryogenic stages of previous missions. The GSLV-F17 has an S139 solid core and four L40H liquid strap-ons. The normal perigee is 172 km and apogee is 29,000 km, but ISRO achieved a 171-km perigee and an apogee of 31,260 km, Narayanan announced on the occasion. The inclination of the satellite is 19.28 degrees, while the payload mass is 2,367 kg, making it the heaviest satellite launched by India so far, he said. articles.title: ISRO Launches EOS-05 Imaging Satellite | GSLV Rocket Mission Sriharikota
articles.content: English News Tech science ISRO Launches EOS 05 Imaging Satellite | GSLV Rocket Mission Sriharikota ISRO launches imaging satellite into space using GSLV rocket: To monitor Pak, China from 36,000 km above; will also aid disaster management Sriharikota 3 hours ago Copy link The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched India’s first EOS-05 imaging satellite at 2:55 am on Thursday using the GSLV-F17 rocket from Sriharikota. The satellite was placed into orbit around 18 minutes after liftoff. The mission comes nearly five years after the failure of GIST-1. The EOS-05 satellite weighs around 2,367 kg. It will take images of large parts of India from an altitude of 36,000 km and will be able to monitor several areas, including the Pakistan-China border. It will also help during disasters. ISRO launched a mission after nearly eight months. Before this, two ISRO launches had failed in January 2026 and March 2025. The EOS-05 satellite was launched aboard the GSLV-F17 rocket. GSLV-F17 was taken to the launchpad at Sriharikota. Mission launched from Sriharikota GSLV-F17 was the 19th flight under India’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle programme. It was launched from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota. The rocket will place EOS-05 into a Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (Sub-GTO). The mission uses a four-metre-diameter ogive composite payload fairing. GISAT-1 mission failed in 2021 In August 2021, ISRO attempted to launch GISAT-1 aboard the GSLV-F10. The mission failed after a problem occurred in the rocket’s cryogenic stage, preventing the satellite from reaching orbit. GISAT-1 was designed to provide near-real-time imaging of the Indian subcontinent from geostationary orbit. ISRO’s previous two launches failed PSLV-C62: On January 12, 2026, the rocket was carrying the DRDO’s ‘Anvesha’ satellite and 15 other co-passenger satellites. However, the mission failed after the rocket became unstable during the third stage. PSLV-C61: On May 18, 2025, the mission aimed to place the Earth observation satellite EOS-09 into orbit. However, the mission failed after a sudden drop in combustion chamber pressure during the third stage. PSLV-C62 was launched at 10:18 on January 12 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. .

articles.title: Nepal floods: India offers DNA tests for immediate relatives of missing people - Firstpost
articles.content: As Nepal struggles to identify hundreds of disaster victims, India has opened its forensic network to families of missing persons India has opened its network of government forensic laboratories to help families identify relatives who went missing in the devastating natural disasters in Nepal. Under the initiative, first-degree biological relatives of missing people can provide DNA samples at designated forensic facilities across India. The samples will be used to help identify unidentified bodies recovered in Nepal. The initiative has been launched by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs in coordination with the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), following flash floods and ice-rock avalanches in Nepal that killed more than 1,200 people and left thousands unaccounted for. Parents, children and siblings of missing persons living in India can provide biological samples for DNA profiling. The move is aimed at speeding up the identification process and helping families get clarity about the fate of their loved ones. Under the new arrangement, eligible relatives can visit designated government forensic facilities to have their samples collected and analysed. The testing will use Autosomal STR (Short Tandem Repeat) DNA profiling, a method widely used in disaster victim identification. The facilities involved include Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs), State Forensic Science Laboratories (SFSLs), laboratories of the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU) in Gandhinagar and its regional campuses, as well as NABL-accredited public forensic institutions. Once the DNA profiles are generated, they will be shared with authorities and disaster victim identification teams in Nepal. The profiles can then be compared with DNA obtained from unidentified remains recovered from the disaster-hit areas. Automated DNA database systems can be used to help identify possible matches. India has also sent a 19-member Disaster Victim Identification (DVI) team to Nepal to support the identification effort on the ground. The team includes forensic scientists and DNA experts from the NFSU and CFSL Delhi. They will work with teams at the Nepal Police Central Forensic Science Laboratory in Kathmandu. The experts will assist with collecting and analysing forensic evidence and matching DNA profiles of missing people with unidentified remains. Identifying victims after large-scale floods, landslides and other natural disasters can be extremely difficult. Bodies may be severely damaged or decomposed, making visual identification unreliable or impossible. In such situations, DNA profiling can provide a more reliable way of establishing a victim’s identity. DNA matches can eventually provide families with confirmation and help authorities ensure that victims are formally identified.

articles.title: ISRO launches India's first -ever geo imaging satellite EOS-05; Gaganyaan up next | WATCH
articles.content: Edited By : Sruthi Paruthikad Last Updated: 04 Sept 2026, 06:38 am IST Share ISRO successfully launched its first-ever geosynchronous earth imaging satellite, EOS-05, aboard a GSLV rocket, with ISRO Chief V Narayanan confirming that preparations for the first uncrewed Gaganyaan spaceflight are in full swing. GSLV-F17/EOS-05 Earth observation satellite which was successfully launched on 04 Sept 2026 at 02:55 AM IST from the Second Launch Pad (SLP) at Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC), SHAR, in Sriharikota on Thursday | Photo: @isro /X Sriharikota (Andhra Pradesh): The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) achieved a historical milestone on Friday by successfully launching the country's first-ever imaging satellite into geo-orbit. Using a GSLV rocket, the space agency precisely injected the 2,300+ kg EOS-05 payload into its target sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit, marking ISRO's first successful mission of the year 2026. The EOS-05 satellite took off from the second launchpad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at 2.55 am following a smooth 27-hour countdown. Operating at an altitude of approximately 36,000 km, the satellite will synchronize with the Earth's rotational speed, serving as an "eye in the sky" to provide near real-time imagery for agriculture, natural disaster monitoring, and strategic national data. Announcing the success, ISRO Chairman V Narayanan stated, “I am very happy to announce that the GSLV F-17 vehicle has successfully and precisely injected the advanced EOS-05 geo imaging satellite in the intended and required orbit.” He highlighted that the mission carried the heaviest payload (2,367 kg) ever delivered by a GSLV rocket. Dismissing speculative reports, Narayanan clarified during a press interaction that EOS-05 is not a “spy satellite” and possesses an operational lifespan of nine years. Following the successful deployment, Narayanan outlined ISRO's future roadmap, confirming that “vigorous, systematic work” is underway to execute the first uncrewed Gaganyaan human spaceflight mission within this calendar year. He noted that the space agency is aiming for six additional launches during the current financial year, including the navigation satellite NVS-03. articles.content: The Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro) on Friday successfully launched a GSLV rocket, carrying the Earth observation satellite EOS-05 from the spaceport in Andhra Pradesh's Sriharikota. The Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro) on Friday successfully launched a GSLV rocket, carrying the Earth observation satellite EOS-05 from the spaceport in Andhra Pradesh's Sriharikota. The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV), on its 19th flight, placed the EOS-05 into the intended Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit 18 minutes after it was launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at 2:55 am. "Mission Success! GSLV-F17 has accomplished its mission, placing EOS-05 into the intended orbit," Isro wrote in a post on X, sharing the photographs from the launch, with the caption: "Sharing a few memorable moments from the lift-off." What makes the mission monumental is the fact that the EOS-05 is India’s first-ever imaging satellite to monitor from Geosynchronous orbit about 36,000 km above the Earth. “I am very happy to announce that the GSLV-F17 vehicle has successfully and precisely injected the advanced Earth observation satellite EOS-05 into the intended and required orbit, “ Isro Chairman Dr V. Narayanan said. In his statement, he mentioned that this was the 107th launch from the spaceport in Sriharikota and the 19th mission of the GSLV. “The first launch of the GSLV- D1 was done with a payload of 1536 kg; from that, we have gradually improved the performance of this vehicle by optimising the structural mass, improving the propulsion systems, and today we have injected the heaviest satellite, a 2367 kg satellite, using this launch vehicle,” he added. The Isro chairman went on to reiterate the significance of the mission. “From the satellite data, we confirm all the valves are operating perfectly, the solar panel is deployed, and the health of the satellite is perfectly alright. "In the coming days, we will raise the orbit and take it to the required orbit and place the satellite in the Geo platform for national activities,” the ISRO Chairman said. It is pertinent to note that the EOS-05 satellite is dubbed as "Eye in the Sky". It is expected to provide real-time imagery, besides helping agriculture, environment, disaster management, among others. This was the first successful launch activity Isro conducted since the failure of the PSLV-C62 mission carrying the EOS-N1 earth observation satellite on January 12, 2026. Before this, the space agency saw back-to-back failures with the launch of PSLV-C62 and PSLV-C61 on May 18, 2025. The EOS-05 satellite will replace the unsuccessful EOS-03 mission. Meanwhile, the Minister of State in the Department of Atomic Energy of India, Jitendra Singh, lauded the Isro team and congratulated them on a successful launch. "Another giant leap for India in Space! Kudos to Team @isro on the successful launch of GSLV-F17/EOS-05," he wrote in his post on X, formerly known as Twitter. "With the visionary leadership of PM Shri @narendramodi Ji, India’s space capabilities continue to scale new heights, strengthening our position as a global space power," he added.

articles.title: Sriharikota: ISRO Roars Back into Action - Deccan Chronicle
articles.content: Sriharikota: In a spectacular early-morning display of technical brilliance, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched the GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) Sriharikota at 2:55 AM on Friday. Leaving a trail of orange flames that pierced the darkness, the 51.7-metre-tall GSLV lifted off majestically from the Second Launch Pad and zoomed into the night sky with textbook precision. The flawless execution sparked immediate celebration, bringing immense delight to scientists at the Mission Control Room and the crowds gathered at the visitors gallery, unmindful of the downpour, to witness the historic event. Weighing 420.5 tonnes at lift-off, the three-stage Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV)—equipped with an indigenous cryogenic upper stage and a 4-metre-diameter ogive composite payload fairing—perfectly deployed the Earth Observation Satellite-05 (EOS-05) into its targeted Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (Sub-GTO). Operating from an altitude of around 36,000 km, EOS-05 marks a monumental milestone as India’s first-ever imaging satellite stationed in a geosynchronous orbit. The state-of-the-art spacecraft is engineered to provide advanced, real-time Earth observation data, vastly strengthening the country's capabilities in land monitoring, environmental tracking, and disaster management. Notably, EOS-05 serves as a highly anticipated replacement for the GISAT-1A satellite, which was lost during a launch failure in 2021. The high-stakes mission was closely watched worldwide, carrying immense weight for India's space program. Following an uncharacteristic seven-month pause triggered by anomalies in two successive PSLV missions—including the PSLV-C62 mission on January 12—ISRO had temporarily halted launches to conduct exhaustive technical reviews. The flawless performance of GSLV-F17 effectively breaks the hiatus, completely restoring momentum and reinforcing global confidence in ISRO’s launch vehicles. With this triumph, ISRO not only puts an end to its brief dry spell but firmly establishes a sophisticated new sentinel in space, marking another giant leap in India's expanding interplanetary and Earth-observation footprint.

articles.title: 'Naughty Boy' Countdown Begins: ISRO's 'Eye In The Sky' Set For 36,000-Km Journey In A ...
articles.content: Updated 4 September 2026 at 03:52 IST ISRO successfully launches EOS-05 aboard GSLV-F17, giving India a new eye in the sky and a major boost after recent launch setbacks. Shruti Sneha Science News 5 min read Follow : ‘Naughty Boy’ Delivers: ISRO Successfully Launches GSLV-F17 Carrying EOS-05, India’s New ‘Eye In The Sky’ | Image: Republic New Delhi: The wait ended at 2:55 am on Friday as the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05 from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, marking a major step forward for India's Earth observation capabilities. The launch comes at an especially crucial time for ISRO. Following a series of setbacks with its Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), which was formerly regarded as one of the world's most reliable rockets, the agency has entered a challenging phase. With the PSLV now grounded while investigations and tests are underway, the success of GSLV-F17 might provide a significant boost to confidence in India's space program. September 3, 2026 However, the two launchers belong to separate families and have different propulsion systems. The PSLV's recent issues are thus not directly related to the GSLV Mk II, allowing Friday's mission to be evaluated on its own technical merits. Why this GSLV mission is being watched closely The GSLV has a complex history. Inside ISRO, it is popularly known as the "naughty boy" because to its inconsistent performance during its development years. Six of the first 18 flights did not complete their missions successfully. However, the same rocket has played a significant part in India's efforts to develop the ability to launch larger satellites. At the heart of this voyage is the indigenous cryogenic engine. During the 1990s, India requested cryogenic technology from Russia, but the US strongly opposed the transfer due to fears about missile proliferation. International regulations eventually stopped India from obtaining the technology it desired. ISRO subsequently tackled the significantly more difficult challenge of developing the technology domestically. Indian scientists had to perfect cryogenic propulsion systems that used liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen at temperatures below minus 250 degrees Celsius. After years of development, testing, failures, and redesigns, India was finally able to create its own cryogenic upper stage. That achievement marked a significant milestone in India's launch program and remains one of the defining technologies of the GSLV Mk II. The rocket's capabilities have also been internationally validated. The GSLV Mk II was tasked with launching NISAR, the world's most costly civilian Earth imaging satellite, demonstrating confidence in the launcher's ability to perform hard missions. Friday's trip will be the nineteenth flight. EOS-05: An eye that can keep watching India The satellite riding aboard GSLV-F17 is critical to the mission's success. EOS-05, also known as GISAT-1A, weighs about 2,367 kg and is intended to operate from geosynchronous orbit, roughly 36,000 kilometers above Earth. A geosynchronous satellite, as opposed to low-Earth orbit satellites, can maintain a continuous observation of the same large area. This makes EOS-05 especially...
